slots.name: Turbopump cycle
slots.role: How the pump that feeds the chamber is driven.

options.name: Gas generator
options.note: A small burner spins the turbine, then its exhaust is dumped overboard. Merlin, Vulcain, F-1.
cons: Throws away 2–3 % of the propellant unburned

options.name: Staged combustion
options.note: The turbine exhaust goes into the main chamber, so nothing is wasted. Higher pressure, higher Isp, far harder to build.

options.name: Expander
options.note: Hydrogen heated in the chamber walls spins the turbine. Gentle and endlessly restartable, but only enough power for a small engine.
cons: Thrust −15 %: the cycle cannot drive a big pump

options.name: Electric pump
options.note: Battery-driven motors spin the pumps. The simplest plumbing there is; the batteries are heavy.

options.name: Pressure-fed (no pump)
options.note: No pump at all: tank pressure pushes propellant into the chamber. Unlimited restarts, but the thick tanks and low pressure cost thrust and Isp.
options.real: AJ10 (Delta II second stage), Apollo SPS

options.name: Full-flow staged combustion
options.note: Two preburners, one fuel-rich and one oxygen-rich, each drive their own pump, and every gram of propellant then burns in the main chamber. The highest pressure and Isp there is, and the hardest engine to build.
pros: Cooler turbines than ordinary staged combustion
options.real: Raptor (SpaceX), the only full-flow engine ever flown

options.name: Combustion tap-off
options.note: A little hot gas is bled from the edge of the main chamber to spin the turbine. No separate gas generator, so fewer parts, but the turbine sees chamber-hot gas.

slots.name: Injector
slots.role: The plate that sprays fuel and oxidizer into the chamber.

options.name: Coaxial swirl
options.note: Hundreds of small elements, oxidizer inside, fuel swirling around it. Smooth combustion.

options.name: Pintle
options.note: One central element: a pin with a sleeve. Deep throttling, cheap to make, hard to make unstable.

options.name: Impinging jets
options.note: Jets of fuel and oxidizer collide and mix. Simple; prone to rough combustion.

slots.name: Nozzle extension
slots.role: The lower skirt of the bell and how it is kept from melting.

options.name: Regeneratively cooled
options.note: Fuel runs through channels in the bell wall before it burns, keeping the metal cool and preheating the fuel.
pros: Runs as long as there is fuel

options.name: Radiatively cooled niobium
options.note: A thin skirt of C-103 niobium that simply glows orange and radiates the heat away. Light; only for vacuum.

options.name: Carbon-carbon skirt
options.note: Woven carbon fibre in a carbon matrix: half the mass of metal and happy at 2,000 °C.
pros: +4 s of Isp from a longer bell

options.name: Extendable nozzle
options.note: A second skirt that slides down after staging, so a huge bell fits in a short interstage.
cons: One more mechanism that must work

options.name: Ablative liner
options.note: A nozzle lined with resin and silica that chars and wears away slowly, carrying the heat off with it. No cooling plumbing at all: cheap, heavy, good for one long burn.
cons: Wears away: one long burn only
options.real: RS-68 (Delta IV), LR87 nozzle extension (Titan II)

slots.name: Igniter
slots.role: How the engine is lit, and how many times.

options.name: Spark torch
options.note: A small spark-lit torch in the chamber wall. Restartable as long as there is power.
cons: Needs power and a pilot flow

options.name: Pyrotechnic
options.note: A one-shot cartridge. The simplest igniter; one start only.

options.name: TEA-TEB slugs
options.note: Chemicals that burst into green flame on contact with oxygen. Reliable relights, limited by how many slugs you carry.

slots.name: Propellant grain
slots.role: The shape of the hole cast through the propellant, which sets the thrust curve.

options.name: Star grain
options.note: A star-shaped bore gives steady thrust the whole burn.

options.name: High-thrust grain
options.note: More burning surface: +15 % thrust, a shorter burn, slightly less Isp.

options.name: Long-burn grain
options.note: Less surface, a long gentle burn: −15 % thrust, +3 s Isp.

options.name: Finocyl grain
options.note: A round bore with long fins cut into the aft end: high thrust at liftoff that tapers off through the sound barrier, when the stack is under the most strain.

options.name: Fixed nozzle
options.note: Bolted straight. The core engine steers.

options.name: Vectoring nozzle
options.note: A flexible seal lets the nozzle swing a few degrees. Needed when the solids give most of the thrust.

options.name: Liquid-injection steering
options.note: A fixed nozzle with a tank of nitrogen tetroxide: squirting it into one side of the exhaust bends the jet. No moving nozzle, but the tank and valves weigh a lot.

options.name: Crushable honeycomb
options.note: Aluminium honeycomb that crushes once. Light and certain.

options.name: Hydraulic struts
options.note: Oil and gas struts that reset. Heavier; reusable.

options.name: Telescoping pistons + crush cores
options.note: Each leg is a telescoping piston with a cartridge of aluminium honeycomb inside: the honeycomb takes the hit, and a fresh cartridge resets the leg for the next flight.

options.name: Small pads
options.note: Fine on rock.

options.name: Large pads
options.note: Snowshoes for dust.

options.name: Wide dish feet
options.note: Big shallow dishes with crushable rims: they spread the weight on loose sand and slide instead of digging in on a sideways touchdown.
pros: Lands on soft or sloping ground

slots.name: Touchdown sensors
slots.role: How the ship knows its feet are on the ground, so the engine cuts at the right moment.

options.name: Radar altimeter only
options.note: The computer cuts the engine on the radar height. A gust or a rock can fool it by half a metre.
cons: The engine may cut a little high or a little late

options.name: Contact probes
options.note: Long thin rods hang below the feet. The moment one touches the ground a light comes on and the crew shuts the engine down: "Contact light!"
pros: Engine cuts at the right moment

options.name: Load cells in every leg
options.note: Strain gauges in each leg weigh the ship as it settles. The computer cuts the engine only when all four legs carry weight, so it never shuts down on one foot.

slots.name: Base heat shield
slots.role: What protects the engine bay from the glowing exhaust that swirls back up under the engines.

options.name: Flexible thermal curtains
options.note: Quilted boots of glass and ceramic fabric around the top of each engine let it swivel while closing the gap to the hot outside.
options.real: Saturn V S-IC flexible curtains, Shuttle RS-25 heat-shield blankets

options.name: Rigid base heat shield
options.note: A plate of heat-resistant metal and ceramic across the whole base, with a sealed hole for each engine. Under a cluster the jets heat each other, so this is where it matters most.
options.real: Saturn V S-IC base heat shield, Falcon 9 Block 5 Octaweb heat shield

options.name: No base shield
options.note: Bare beams and plumbing. A single engine in thin air gets away with it; a cluster cooks its own wiring.
options.real: Early sounding rockets; N1's first two launches (1969) ended in fires among the 30 engines of its tail

slots.name: Propellant feed
slots.role: The pipes that bring fuel and oxygen from the tanks to each engine.

options.name: Separate feed lines
options.note: One pipe of each propellant to each engine, opened at ignition and closed at the end.
cons: A leaking engine cannot be cut off from its tank

options.name: Manifold with prevalves
options.note: A ring manifold feeds every engine through its own shut-off valve, so the computer can isolate a failing engine and the rest fly on.
options.real: Saturn V S-IC prevalves, Falcon 9 engine-out shutdowns

slots.name: POGO suppressor
slots.role: Stops the engines and the feed lines from shaking each other like a pogo stick.

options.name: Plain feed lines
options.note: Nothing in the lines. If the thrust shake and the sloshing in the pipes fall in step, the whole stack bounces along its length.

options.name: Gas-filled accumulators
options.note: Small helium-filled chambers on the oxygen lines act as shock absorbers and break the rhythm. Fitted to the Saturn V after Apollo 6 shook at 5 Hz and Apollo 13 nearly tore an engine loose.
options.real: Saturn V S-IC and S-II (after Apollo 6 and 13), Titan II for Gemini

slots.name: Chambers
slots.role: How the booster engine burns its kerosene and oxygen.

options.name: Four chambers, one pump
options.note: Four small chambers fed by one turbopump, plus two swivelling verniers. Korolev chose four small chambers because big ones shook themselves apart.

options.name: One big chamber
options.note: One large chamber and nozzle: lighter and cheaper, but big chambers are prone to combustion instability, which took the F-1 years of tests to cure.

options.name: Hydrogen peroxide steam
options.note: Concentrated hydrogen peroxide flows over a bed of solid catalyst pellets and turns into hot steam that spins the turbine. Separate from the main propellants, so it starts easily.

options.name: Gas generator
options.note: A small burner on the main kerosene and oxygen spins the turbine. No peroxide tank to carry.
